title: Chest pain — myocardial infarction / IHD & CABG
scenario: A 45-year-old man comes to the ER because of chest pain. 439B · 439F
A patient with chest pain that comes only during exercise, never at rest. 437A

imgs.cap: Same angiogram labelled — LAD occluded distal to the 1st diagonal Coronary angiogram branch

qs.q: Take a brief history.
a: Pain (SOCRATES): site, onset, character (ischaemia: crushing, retrosternal, "band"/"someone sitting on my chest"; dissection: sharp, tearing; pneumothorax: sudden, sharp, pleuritic; reflux: burning), radiation (left arm/jaw vs back between the shoulder blades), aggravating/relieving, severity.
Associated: nausea, vomiting, sweating, palpitations, dyspnoea, leg swelling, haemoptysis, fever; constitutional symptoms.
Risk factors: smoking, DM, HTN, hypercholesterolaemia, family history, previous IHD/stroke. PMH, medications, surgeries, family & social history.
qs.why: SOCRATES of chest pain separates ischaemic, aortic, pleural and oesophageal causes; associated symptoms and risk factors support the diagnosis.
hist: Crushing retrosternal pain = ischaemia; tearing pain = aortic dissection; sharp pleuritic = pneumothorax/PE; burning = reflux.
Sudden onset suggests dissection, pneumothorax or PE.
Left arm or jaw = cardiac; back between the shoulder blades = dissection.
Exertion and rest point to angina; breathing and position point to pleuritic or pericardial pain.
Smoking, DM, HTN, hypercholesterolaemia, family history
Previous IHD or stroke, medications, surgeries
Known vascular disease and current drugs (antiplatelets, anticoagulants) affect management.

qs.q: What is your (single) most likely diagnosis?
a: MI (acute coronary syndrome / unstable angina).
qs.why: Crushing central pain radiating to the arm/jaw with sweating in a man with risk factors = acute coronary syndrome.

qs.q: What are the life-threatening DDx of sudden-onset chest pain? (must say all)
a: MI, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, oesophageal rupture.
qs.why: These five kill quickly and must be excluded in every chest pain: ACS, dissection, PE, tension pneumothorax, oesophageal rupture.

qs.q: What further investigations would you order?
a: ECG, troponins, echo; gold standard: coronary angiography.
qs.why: ECG and troponin diagnose ACS; echo shows wall motion; coronary angiography defines the anatomy and allows treatment.

qs.q: Troponin and ECG are negative — what else will you do?
a: Stress test.
qs.why: A negative ECG/troponin doesn't exclude coronary disease — stress testing provokes ischaemia to unmask it.

qs.q: What is a stress test?
a: Provoking ischaemia under monitoring: exercise (treadmill) ECG, or pharmacological stress (dobutamine echo / nuclear perfusion) — positive if ischaemic ECG changes, symptoms or wall- motion/perfusion defects.
qs.why: Exercise or drugs increase myocardial demand; ischaemia then shows on ECG, echo wall motion or nuclear perfusion.

qs.q: The stress test is positive — what next?
a: Coronary angiography ± PCI (answer given: PCI).
qs.why: A positive stress test means significant coronary disease — angiography confirms it and allows PCI.

qs.q: What is the best investigation in this case?
a: Coronary angiography.
qs.why: Coronary angiography is the gold standard for coronary anatomy.

qs.q: What is your management?
a: Start with medical treatment (MONA-BASH): pain control, antiplatelet therapy, statins (+ O₂ if hypoxic, nitrates, β-blocker, ACE-I, heparin).
qs.why: Initial ACS treatment relieves pain, prevents thrombus growth (antiplatelets, heparin), reduces demand (β-blocker, nitrates) and stabilises plaque (statin).

qs.q: What are the indications for CABG?
a: Left main stenosis > 50 %.
Left-main equivalent (proximal LAD + circumflex).
Triple-vessel disease (especially with LV dysfunction or diabetes).
Failed PCI.
qs.why: CABG improves survival over PCI when a large area of myocardium is at risk: left main, its equivalent, triple-vessel disease (especially with diabetes or poor LV), or failed PCI.

qs.q: What is the choice of conduits in CABG?
a: Arterial: internal thoracic (mammary) artery, radial artery (after Allen's test). Venous: long (great) saphenous vein.
qs.why: Arterial conduits last longest (internal mammary, radial if Allen's test shows good ulnar supply); the saphenous vein is long and easily harvested.

qs.q: Why choose the internal thoracic artery? (not in all tracks)
a: Best long-term patency, resistant to atherosclerosis (endothelial nitric oxide), stays open for life.
qs.why: The internal mammary artery resists atherosclerosis and stays patent in > 90% at 10 years, especially to the LAD.

qs.q: The patient has chest pain on exercise and never at rest — what is the diagnosis?
a: Stable angina.
qs.why: Pain only on exertion and relieved by rest = stable angina (fixed stenosis); pain at rest suggests ACS.

notes.t: The cardiac cases in the 437 file were written from the IHD/valve lectures (first year as an OSCE topic), so they are not counted as exam appearances.

extra.q: Angiogram shown (reporters weren't sure it was shown): What is this investigation? What are the findings?
a: Coronary angiography — the left anterior descending artery is occluded (see labelled picture).

title: Thoracic aorta — aortic regurgitation, ascending aneurysm & dissection
scenario: A 35-year-old man found to have an early diastolic murmur at the 2nd right intercostal space on routine check-up. 438F
A patient with symptoms and signs of heart failure and an early diastolic murmur. 439A

qs.q: What is your differential diagnosis?
a: Aortic valve regurgitation.
qs.why: An early diastolic murmur at the right 2nd ICS = aortic regurgitation.

qs.q: What investigations would you order?
a: ECG, echocardiography, chest X-ray (+ labs: CBC, coagulation).
qs.why: Echo grades the regurgitation and measures the aortic root; CXR may show a dilated aorta or cardiomegaly.

qs.q: The CXR shows a widened mediastinum — what is the diagnosis / next step?
a: Ascending aortic aneurysm → CT (angiography) of the chest.
qs.why: AR with a widened mediastinum suggests dilatation of the ascending aorta — CT angiography defines it.

qs.q: At what diameter do you operate on the ascending aorta?
a: ≥ 5.5 cm (≥ 5.0 cm in Marfan/bicuspid valve, or growth > 0.5 cm/year).
qs.why: Above 5.5 cm (lower in Marfan/bicuspid) or with rapid growth, rupture/dissection risk exceeds surgical risk.

qs.q: What are the two most feared complications if left untreated?
a: Aortic dissection and rupture.
qs.why: A dilated aorta can tear (dissection) or burst (rupture) — both often fatal.

qs.q: What are the types of aortic dissection, and the name of the classification?
a: Stanford: type A (involves the ascending aorta — emergency surgery) and type B (descending only — medical/TEVAR). (DeBakey I–III.)
qs.why: Stanford classifies by whether the ascending aorta is involved — type A needs emergency surgery (risk of tamponade, AR, coronary occlusion), type B is usually managed medically.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: Ascending aorta replacement (graft) ± valve repair/replacement.
qs.why: The dilated ascending aorta is replaced with a graft, with the valve repaired or replaced if regurgitant.

qs.q: Aortic aneurysm on CT — give 3 DDx.
a: Aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, intramural haematoma (penetrating ulcer).
qs.why: Aneurysm, dissection and intramural haematoma are the acute aortic pathologies to distinguish on CT.

qs.q: When do you admit the patient?
a: Symptomatic (chest/back pain), signs of rupture or dissection, haemodynamic instability, rapid expansion.
qs.why: Pain, instability or rapid growth suggest impending rupture or dissection — admit for urgent management.

qs.q: What are the indications for surgery?
a: Rupture, symptoms, diameter above threshold (ascending ≥ 5.5 cm; descending ≥ 6 cm; AAA ≥ 5.5 cm), rapid growth (> 0.5 cm/year thoracic; ≥ 1 cm/year AAA).
qs.why: Thresholds differ by segment; rupture, symptoms or rapid growth are indications regardless of size.

qs.q: What is the management? (3)
a: Risk-factor & BP control with surveillance imaging; open surgical graft replacement; endovascular repair (TEVAR/EVAR).
qs.why: Small stable aneurysms are watched with BP control; large/symptomatic ones are repaired open or endovascularly.

notes.t: The 438F file wrote "5" — the usual threshold is 5.5 cm (5.0 cm in Marfan / bicuspid valve).

title: Aortic stenosis
scenario: A 65-year-old with exertional dyspnoea and chest pain for 2 years; pulse 80/min; harsh ejection systolic murmur at the 2nd right intercostal space. (441A station 6 shared this page of the file) 441A

qs.q: What is the likely diagnosis?
a: Aortic valve stenosis.
qs.why: Exertional dyspnoea/angina with an ejection systolic murmur at the right 2nd ICS (radiating to the carotids) = aortic stenosis.

qs.q: What are the aetiologies?
a: Degenerative (calcific/sclerosis), bicuspid aortic valve (congenital), rheumatic fever.
qs.why: Calcific degeneration in the elderly, a bicuspid valve in younger patients, and rheumatic disease.

qs.q: What investigations would you order?
a: Echocardiography (TTE or TOE), ECG, chest X-ray, cardiac catheterisation.
qs.why: Echo is the key test (valve area, gradient, LV function); ECG/CXR show LVH; catheterisation assesses coronaries before surgery.

qs.q: What are the indications for surgery?
a: Symptomatic severe AS; asymptomatic AS with reduced ejection fraction; asymptomatic AS undergoing cardiac surgery for another indication.
qs.why: Once severe AS causes symptoms (angina, syncope, heart failure), survival falls sharply without valve replacement.

qs.q: What are the surgical options?
a: Surgical aortic valve replacement; transcatheter AVR (TAVR/TAVI); percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty (children/young adults without calcification).
qs.why: Surgical AVR is standard; TAVI for older/high-risk patients; balloon valvuloplasty mainly for young non-calcified valves.

title: Aortic intramural haematoma (CT)
scenario: Cardiac surgery case (new) — CT image of the thoracic aorta. 438A

imgs.cap: Sagittal CT angiogram of the thoracic aorta — intramural haematoma

qs.q: What do you see?
a: Dilated aorta with an intramural (crescentic wall) collection.
qs.why: A crescentic thickening of the aortic wall without an intimal flap is an intramural haematoma.

qs.q: Mention 3 differential diagnoses.
a: Aortic intramural haematoma, aortic dissection, aortic aneurysm.
qs.why: IMH, dissection and aneurysm look similar — the intimal flap (dissection) and wall thickening (IMH) separate them.

qs.q: What is the treatment?
a: Surgery (repair) — especially when the ascending aorta is involved (type A).
qs.why: IMH behaves like dissection: ascending involvement (type A) needs surgery, descending is managed medically.

title: Post-CABG mediastinitis
scenario: A patient developed fever with local erythema and tenderness around the sternal wound after CABG — acute (necrotising) mediastinitis. Questions were about history & examination findings and management. 439B

qs.q: What will you find on history and examination?
a: Fever, chest pain, wound erythema, tenderness, purulent discharge, sternal instability ("click"), tachycardia/sepsis.
qs.why: Deep sternal wound infection presents with fever, wound inflammation and discharge, and an unstable sternum.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: Blood & wound cultures, CT chest; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics; surgical debridement (sternal wound exploration, removal of wires/infected tissue), drainage/irrigation or negative-pressure therapy, then delayed closure / muscle-flap reconstruction.
qs.why: Mediastinitis is a deep infection with high mortality: cultures and CT, IV antibiotics, and surgical debridement with drainage/negative pressure, then flap closure.

title: Mitral stenosis
scenario: A 27-year-old man with a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur and a history of rheumatic fever in childhood. (lecture-based case — not yet asked)

qs.q: What is the likely diagnosis?
a: Mitral stenosis.
qs.why: Rumbling mid-diastolic murmur with a rheumatic history = mitral stenosis.

qs.q: What are the aetiologies?
a: Rheumatic fever (most common), mitral annular calcification (degenerative), congenital.
qs.why: Rheumatic fever causes most MS (fused commissures); annular calcification in the elderly.

qs.q: What investigations would you order?
a: Echocardiography (TTE/TOE), ECG, chest X-ray, cardiac catheterisation.
qs.why: Echo measures valve area and suitability for balloon valvotomy; TOE excludes left atrial thrombus.

qs.q: What is the best management option for most patients?
a: Percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy (PMBC).
qs.why: Pliable rheumatic valves split well along the fused commissures with a balloon — avoiding open surgery.

qs.q: What are the contraindications to this procedure?
a: Left-atrial thrombus (AF), significant mitral regurgitation, bi-commissural calcification.
qs.why: LA thrombus can embolise during the procedure; significant MR worsens; heavy commissural calcification won't split.

qs.q: Alternative if PMBC isn't possible and MS is severe and symptomatic?
a: Mitral valve surgery: open commissurotomy or valve replacement (mechanical or bioprosthetic).
qs.why: When balloon valvotomy isn't possible, the valve is opened surgically or replaced.

title: Prosthetic heart valves
scenario: Picture of a prosthetic heart valve. (lecture-based case — not yet asked)

qs.q: What is this?
a: A prosthetic heart valve.
qs.why: The ring and leaflets/disc identify a prosthetic heart valve.

qs.q: Mention 2 types.
a: Mechanical and biological (bioprosthetic).
qs.why: Valves are either mechanical or biological (tissue).

qs.q: What is the difference?
a: Biological: lasts ~8–10 years, no lifelong anticoagulation, no click — for elderly, women wanting pregnancy, bleeding risk / poor compliance.
Mechanical: lasts > 20 years, lifelong warfarin, audible click — for young patients.
qs.why: Mechanical valves are durable but thrombogenic (lifelong warfarin); tissue valves avoid anticoagulation but degenerate — so choice depends on age, pregnancy plans and bleeding risk.
